paragraphs.paraphrase: Next they reached the island of Aeolus, son of Hippotas, a favorite of the gods. The island seems to float on the sea and is ringed by an iron wall. Aeolus has six sons and six daughters and married the sons to the daughters; they all live with their parents in endless feasting, the house full of the smell of roasting meat by day, each couple sleeping together at night.

barriers.quote: an island that floats (as it were) upon the sea
barriers.my_reading: either a truly floating island or one that only seems to float
barriers.note: '(as it were)' leaves it unclear whether this is literal

barriers.quote: an iron-bound wall
barriers.my_reading: a wall made of, or reinforced with, iron

barriers.quote: he made the sons marry the daughters
barriers.my_reading: he married his sons to their own sisters
barriers.note: a reader may reread to check that it really means brother-sister marriage; the text passes over it without comment

barriers.quote: till the whole place groans with it, yard and all
barriers.my_reading: the house and courtyard are heavy with the smell of cooking, or perhaps echo with the noise of feasting
barriers.note: 'groans' could mean overloaded or noisy

paragraphs.paraphrase: Aeolus hosted Odysseus for a month, asking all about Troy and the Greeks' return, and when Odysseus asked for help to leave he gave it readily: Zeus had made him keeper of the winds, so he shut the storm winds in a bag made from an ox hide, tied it tightly with silver thread aboard the ship, and left only the favorable West wind free to blow. But the men's own foolishness ruined everything.

barriers.quote: the Argive fleet
barriers.my_reading: the Greek fleet at Troy
barriers.note: 'Argive' is not explained and appears beside 'Achaeans' as another name for the Greeks

barriers.quote: He flayed me a prime ox hide to hold the paths of the roaring winds
barriers.my_reading: he skinned an ox and made its hide into a bag to hold the winds
barriers.note: 'flayed me' (= for me) is archaic, and it is hard to picture 'paths of the winds' being put in a bag

barriers.quote: The West wind, which was fair for us, he alone let blow as it chose
barriers.my_reading: he let only the West wind, which was favorable, blow freely
barriers.note: inverted word order; 'fair' = favorable

paragraphs.paraphrase: After nine days they came in sight of home, close enough to see fires burning on the land. Exhausted from steering the whole way himself, Odysseus fell asleep, and his men grumbled that he was bringing home gold and silver from Aeolus in the bag while they, after the same hardships, had nothing, so they decided to open it and see.

barriers.quote: we could see the stubble fires burning
barriers.my_reading: they could see farmers burning dry stalks in the fields after harvest

paragraphs.paraphrase: The men opened the bag; the winds burst out in a storm that swept them, weeping, away from their homeland. Odysseus woke and considered drowning himself but chose to endure, lying covered up in the ship while the winds blew the fleet back to Aeolus's island.

barriers.quote: covered myself up
barriers.my_reading: he pulled his cloak over his head in despair
barriers.note: the meaning of the gesture is not explained

paragraphs.paraphrase: Back on the island, after fetching water and eating, Odysseus took a herald and one companion to Aeolus's palace, where the family was feasting, and they sat on the threshold as suppliants. Astonished, the family asked why he had come back and which god was persecuting him, since they had done so much to send him home.

barriers.quote: I took a herald
barriers.my_reading: an official messenger or attendant who goes with a leader on formal visits
barriers.note: his role is not explained

barriers.quote: we sat down as suppliants on the threshold
barriers.my_reading: they sat humbly in the doorway as formal petitioners begging for help
barriers.note: the custom behind the gesture is not explained

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus answers sadly that his men, and his untimely sleep, have ruined him, and begs the family to repair the damage, which they have the power to do.

barriers.quote: mend me this mischief
barriers.my_reading: repair this harm for me
barriers.note: archaic; 'mischief' here means serious harm, not naughtiness

paragraphs.paraphrase: The family is silent; then Aeolus calls Odysseus the vilest of men, orders him off the island, refuses to help anyone the gods so plainly hate, and sends him away.

barriers.quote: I will help no man whom heaven hates
barriers.my_reading: Aeolus takes Odysseus's disaster as proof that the gods hate him, so helping him again would offend them
barriers.note: the reasoning is left implied

paragraphs.paraphrase: With no wind, the men rowed for six days; on the seventh they reached Telepylus, the rocky fortress of Lamus and city of the Laestrygonians. There a herdsman bringing his flock home is greeted by another taking his out, and a man who needed no sleep could earn two wages, one herding cattle and one herding sheep, because people work by night much as by day.

barriers.quote: the rocky stronghold of Lamus—Telepylus, the city of the Laestrygonians
barriers.my_reading: Telepylus is the city, the Laestrygonians are its people, and Lamus is perhaps its founder or ruler
barriers.note: who Lamus is is never explained

barriers.quote: the shepherd driving in his sheep and goats to be milked greets the one driving out his flock to feed
barriers.my_reading: the nights are so short that the herdsman coming home in the evening meets the one setting out in the morning
barriers.note: the point of this detail is never stated

barriers.quote: a man who could do without sleep might earn double wages
barriers.my_reading: because it is light nearly all the time, someone who did not sleep could hold a day job and a night job

paragraphs.paraphrase: The harbor was almost enclosed by steep cliffs, with a narrow entrance between two headlands and dead-calm water inside; the other captains moored their ships close together inside, but Odysseus tied his own ship to a rock outside, at the tip of the headland. From a high rock he saw no people or farm animals, only smoke rising, so he sent two men and an attendant to find out who lived there.

barriers.quote: we found it landlocked under steep cliffs
barriers.my_reading: the harbor was almost completely enclosed by land and cliffs
barriers.note: 'landlocked' usually describes countries without a coast

barriers.quote: made them fast close to one another
barriers.my_reading: tied the ships up side by side
barriers.note: nautical

paragraphs.paraphrase: The scouts followed the road used to haul firewood into town and met a girl fetching water from the spring Artacia, daughter of a Laestrygonian named Antiphates. When they asked who the king was, she sent them to her father's house, where they found his wife, a giantess as big as a mountain, and were horrified.

barriers.quote: She directed them to her father’s house
barriers.my_reading: her father Antiphates is the king they asked about
barriers.note: implied, never stated

barriers.quote: the fountain Artacia
barriers.my_reading: a natural spring that serves as the town's water source
barriers.note: 'fountain' in the old sense of spring

paragraphs.paraphrase: The giantess summoned Antiphates from the meeting place; he grabbed one of the men and began eating him, while the other two fled to the ships. At his shout thousands of giant Laestrygonians came running, hurled rocks from the cliffs that smashed the ships together, and speared the men like fish to carry home and eat. Odysseus cut his own ship's mooring rope with his sword and his crew rowed desperately out to sea; every other ship and its crew was destroyed.

barriers.quote: raised a hue and cry after them
barriers.my_reading: raised a loud alarm and called people to chase them
barriers.note: old idiom

barriers.quote: So they laid out for their lives
barriers.my_reading: they rowed as hard as they could to save their lives
barriers.note: 'laid out' = pulled hard at the oars

barriers.quote: As for the others, there was not one of them left
barriers.my_reading: all the other ships inside the harbor were destroyed with their crews, leaving only Odysseus's ship
barriers.note: the scale of the loss is stated only this briefly, and the size of the fleet is not restated in this Book

paragraphs.paraphrase: They sailed on, grieving, and reached the Aeaean island, home of Circe, a powerful and cunning goddess, sister of the sorcerer Aeetes; both are children of the Sun and of Perse, daughter of Oceanus. Guided by some god, they landed and lay exhausted for two days. On the third morning Odysseus climbed a lookout, saw smoke rising from Circe's house in a thick forest, and decided to go back to the ship, feed his men and send a scouting party rather than go himself.

barriers.quote: own sister to the magician Aeetes, for they are both children of the sun by Perse, who is daughter to Oceanus
barriers.my_reading: Circe and Aeetes are full siblings; their father is the Sun, a god, and their mother is Perse, whose father is Oceanus
barriers.note: 'by Perse' = with Perse as mother; who Oceanus is is not said

barriers.quote: We brought our ship into a safe harbor without a word
barriers.my_reading: they came into harbor in silence, perhaps from exhaustion and grief, or because a god guided them without their needing to steer
barriers.note: the point of 'without a word' is unclear

paragraphs.paraphrase: On his way back, a god sent a huge stag into his path as it came down to drink; Odysseus speared it through the back, tied its legs with a rope he twisted from grass and reeds, and carried it slung round his neck, leaning on his spear. At the ship he cheered up each of the men: they would not starve after all. They uncovered their heads, admired the stag, and cooked it.

barriers.quote: we are not going to die so much before our time after all
barriers.my_reading: we are not going to die early (of hunger) after all
barriers.note: 'so much before our time' is awkward

barriers.quote: they uncovered their heads on the seashore
barriers.my_reading: they had been lying with their heads covered in despair and now uncovered them
barriers.note: the covering was never mentioned, and the gesture is not explained

paragraphs.paraphrase: They feasted all day and slept on the shore. At dawn Odysseus held a council: they are in serious trouble, so lost that they cannot tell east from west, but they must find a way out. He has seen that they are on a low island surrounded by sea, with smoke rising from a forest in the middle.

barriers.quote: We have no idea where the sun either sets or rises, so we do not even know East from West
barriers.my_reading: they are completely disoriented and cannot work out which way home lies
barriers.note: taken literally it is puzzling, since they can see the sun rise

barriers.quote: I went as high as I could this morning
barriers.my_reading: he means the climb described in ¶11
barriers.note: that climb was on the previous morning, so 'this morning' confuses the timeline

paragraphs.paraphrase: The men despaired, remembering Antiphates and Polyphemus, and wept. Odysseus split them into two companies, one under Eurylochus and one under himself; they drew lots in a helmet to decide which would go, and Eurylochus set out with his twenty-two men, everyone weeping.

barriers.quote: Their hearts sank as they heard me
barriers.my_reading: the smoke means there are inhabitants, and their last encounters with locals were deadly
barriers.note: the connection is left for the reader to make

barriers.quote: Then we cast lots in a helmet, and the lot fell on Eurylochus
barriers.my_reading: they shook tokens in a helmet to decide which company would go to investigate the smoke
barriers.note: what the lot decides is not stated

paragraphs.paraphrase: Circe's stone house stood in a clearing visible from afar. Wolves and lions, tamed by her drugs and spells, fawned on the men like dogs greeting a master who brings them scraps, which frightened the men. At the gate they heard Circe singing at her loom, weaving a beautiful fabric, and Polites, Odysseus's most trusted man, suggested calling out to see whether she was a woman or a goddess.

barriers.quote: on a site that could be seen from far off, in the middle of the forest
barriers.my_reading: the house stood in a clearing or on high ground inside the forest
barriers.note: hard to picture something visible from afar in a dense forest

barriers.quote: poor bewitched creatures whom she had tamed by her enchantments and drugged into submission
barriers.my_reading: animals tamed by her magic, possibly men she has transformed
barriers.note: whether they were once men is only hinted at later (¶34)

barriers.quote: making a web so fine
barriers.my_reading: weaving a piece of cloth
barriers.note: 'web' may suggest a spider's web

paragraphs.paraphrase: Circe invited them in; all went except the suspicious Eurylochus. She seated them and gave them a mixture of cheese, honey, grain and wine drugged to make them forget home, then struck them with her wand, turning them into pigs, and penned them in her sties: pigs in body, but with their human minds and memories intact.

barriers.quote: mixed them a mess with cheese, honey, meal, and Pramnian wine
barriers.my_reading: made them a mixed dish or drink of cheese, honey, ground grain and a particular kind of wine
barriers.note: 'mess' = a dish of food and 'meal' = ground grain; both have misleading modern meanings

paragraphs.paraphrase: Circe threw the pigs acorns and beechnuts, while Eurylochus rushed back to Odysseus, so overcome that for a while he could only weep, until they got the story out of him.

barriers.quote: beech mast
barriers.my_reading: nuts fallen from beech trees
barriers.note: the context ('such as pigs eat') helps

paragraphs.paraphrase: Eurylochus reports: they found the stone house in the forest and a woman or goddess singing at her loom; she invited them in and the others went, but he stayed outside suspecting a trap, and although he waited a long time, none of them came out.

Odysseus armed himself with sword and bow and ordered Eurylochus to lead him back, but Eurylochus clutched him and begged to stay, predicting that Odysseus would neither rescue the men nor return himself, and urging that the survivors escape while they could.
Odysseus tells Eurylochus to stay at the ship eating and drinking, but says he himself must go, because duty compels him.

barriers.quote: I am most urgently bound to do so
barriers.my_reading: I am under a strong obligation to go
barriers.note: 'bound' = obliged, not the modern 'certain to'

paragraphs.paraphrase: Walking inland, near Circe's house, Odysseus met the god Hermes, disguised as a young man. Hermes told him his men were penned in Circe's pigsties and that on his own he would never free them and would be trapped himself, but offered to protect him with a powerful herb to carry into her house as a charm against harm.

barriers.quote: I met Hermes with his golden wand, disguised as a young man
barriers.my_reading: the god Hermes appeared in the form of a young man; Odysseus, telling the story later, knows who he was
barriers.note: how Odysseus recognized a disguised god, and why Hermes helps him, is not explained

barriers.quote: Take this herb, which is one of great virtue
barriers.my_reading: an herb with great power
barriers.note: 'virtue' = power or potency, not moral goodness; recurs in ¶22

paragraphs.paraphrase: Hermes explains Circe's methods: she will give Odysseus a drugged drink, but the herb will make him immune. When she strikes him with her wand he should draw his sword and lunge as if to kill her; frightened, she will invite him to bed. He should not refuse, since he wants her to free his men and treat him well, but he must first make her swear by the gods to plot no more harm, or once he is naked she will rob him of his manhood.

barriers.quote: she will drug the meal she makes it with
barriers.my_reading: she will drug the ground grain she mixes into the drink
barriers.note: 'meal' reads as 'a meal' (dinner) unless the reader remembers the grain in ¶16

barriers.quote: she will strip you of your manhood and leave you helpless
barriers.my_reading: she will take away your virility or strength, possibly by castrating you
barriers.note: unclear whether this is literal or figurative

paragraphs.paraphrase: Hermes pulls the herb from the ground and shows it to him: black root, milk-white flower, called Moly by the gods; mortals cannot uproot it, but gods can do anything.

Hermes returned to Olympus, and Odysseus, anxious, went on to Circe's house. She invited him in, seated him on a fine chair, gave him a drugged drink in a golden cup, and when it had no effect struck him with her wand, ordering him off to the pigsty with the others.

Odysseus rushed at her with his sword; she screamed, fell and clasped his knees, begging to know who he was, since no man had ever resisted her drug. She guessed he must be Odysseus, whose coming Hermes had foretold, and invited him to put away his sword and come to bed so that they could learn to trust each other.

barriers.quote: clasped my knees
barriers.my_reading: a gesture of begging for mercy
barriers.note: the custom is not explained

barriers.quote: a taste of the herb I gave you
barriers.my_reading: her own drugged potion, not Hermes's protective herb
barriers.note: 'herb' was just used for Hermes's Moly, so the two are easily confused

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus says he cannot be friendly with someone who has just turned his men into pigs, suspects the invitation to bed is a trap to unman him, and refuses unless she first swears a solemn oath to do him no further harm.

barriers.quote: will unman me and make me fit for nothing
barriers.my_reading: take away his manhood, leaving him weak or impotent
barriers.note: same ambiguity as in ¶22

paragraphs.paraphrase: Circe swore the oath as he demanded, and then he went to bed with her.

Meanwhile her four maidservants, spirits born of groves, springs and rivers, prepared the house: one covered a seat with purple cloth over a rug, one set silver tables with gold baskets, one mixed wine with water in a silver bowl and set out gold cups, and one heated water and bathed Odysseus, then oiled him, dressed him and seated him. A maid brought water for his hands and a senior servant brought food, but when Circe invited him to eat he sat refusing, gloomy and suspicious.

barriers.quote: They are the children of the groves and fountains, and of the holy waters that run down into the sea
barriers.my_reading: they are nature spirits born of woods, springs and rivers
barriers.note: unclear whether this is meant literally

barriers.quote: An upper servant
barriers.my_reading: a senior household servant, such as a housekeeper
barriers.note: unclear whether this servant and the maid are extra to the four already described

paragraphs.paraphrase: Circe asks why he sits silent, brooding and refusing food: is he still suspicious, when she has sworn not to harm him?
Odysseus answers that no decent man could eat or drink before his friends were freed; if she wants him to eat, she must free his men and let him see them with his own eyes.

Circe went to the sties with her wand and let out the men, who looked like fattened hogs, then rubbed each with a second drug so that their bristles fell off and they became men again, younger, taller and handsomer than before. They recognized Odysseus, clasped his hand and wept for joy; moved, Circe told Odysseus to go back, haul his ship ashore, hide its gear in a cave, and bring the rest of his crew.

barriers.quote: the whole house was filled with the sound of their hallooing
barriers.my_reading: their loud shouting and crying
barriers.note: archaic

barriers.quote: My men came out like so many prime hogs
barriers.my_reading: they came out looking like big, well-fattened pigs
barriers.note: odd to say 'like' when at this point they actually are pigs

paragraphs.paraphrase: At the ship, the weeping crew crowded round Odysseus as joyfully as penned calves running out to their mothers coming home in the evening, as glad as if they had reached Ithaca itself, and asked what had happened to their comrades.

barriers.quote: as calves break out and gambol round their mothers
barriers.my_reading: like calves that burst out of their pen and frisk around the cows coming home
barriers.note: 'gambol' (frolic) and 'lowing' (mooing) are uncommon words

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus reassures them and tells them to haul the ship ashore, hide its gear and their goods in a cave, and come with him to Circe's house, where their comrades are feasting.

Eurylochus tries to stop them, warning that Circe will turn them all into pigs, wolves or lions to guard her house, and reminding them that Odysseus's recklessness got their comrades killed in the Cyclops's cave.

barriers.quote: who will turn us all into pigs or wolves or lions, and we shall have to keep guard over her house
barriers.my_reading: the wolves and lions around her house were once men whom she transformed and who now guard it
barriers.note: this confirms the hint in ¶15 only indirectly

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus was tempted to draw his sword and cut off Eurylochus's head, even though they were close relatives, but the men pleaded for him and suggested that Eurylochus stay to guard the ship while the rest went.

barriers.quote: in spite of his being a near relation of my own
barriers.my_reading: Eurylochus is a close relative of Odysseus
barriers.note: the exact relationship is not given and has not been mentioned before

paragraphs.paraphrase: They all went inland, and Eurylochus came too, afraid after Odysseus's harsh rebuke.

barriers.quote: the severe reprimand I had given him
barriers.my_reading: Odysseus must have spoken harshly to him, though only his murderous thought was described
barriers.note: no reprimand is actually reported

paragraphs.paraphrase: Meanwhile Circe had had the rescued men bathed, oiled and clothed, and the newcomers found them at dinner; the two groups recognized each other and wept aloud. Circe told Odysseus to stop the weeping: their suffering at sea and among savages was over, and they should stay, eating and drinking, until they recovered the strength and spirits they had when they left Ithaca.

barriers.quote: the men who had been left behind
barriers.my_reading: the men who had been pigs and stayed at Circe's house, not the ones left at the ship
barriers.note: earlier, 'left behind' referred to the men at the ship

barriers.quote: till the whole palace rang again
barriers.my_reading: until the palace echoed
barriers.note: 'again' = echoing, not a second time

paragraphs.paraphrase: They agreed and stayed with Circe a full year, feasting. When the year had come round, the men took Odysseus aside and told him it was time to think of home, if he ever meant to see it again.

barriers.quote: when the year had passed in the waning of moons and the long days had come round
barriers.my_reading: after the months had passed and the long summer days had returned, a full year later
barriers.note: poetic time phrase

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus agreed. After a day of feasting, while the men slept in a covered part of the house, Odysseus, in bed with Circe, formally begged her to keep her promise to help him home, since he and his men wanted to go and the men kept complaining to him.

barriers.quote: the covered gallery
barriers.my_reading: a roofed porch or colonnade
barriers.note: modern 'gallery' suggests an art gallery

barriers.quote: entreated her by her knees
barriers.my_reading: begged her in the formal manner of a suppliant, as if clasping her knees
barriers.note: strange to picture in bed

barriers.quote: please keep the promise you made me
barriers.my_reading: a promise to help him home that she must have made earlier
barriers.note: no such promise appears in this Book

paragraphs.paraphrase: Circe agrees that none of them need stay, but says Odysseus must first make another journey: to the land of the dead ruled by Hades and Persephone, to consult the ghost of the blind prophet Tiresias of Thebes, the only dead man whom Persephone allowed to keep his wits; the other ghosts drift about mindlessly.

barriers.quote: the house of Hades and of dread Persephone
barriers.my_reading: the underworld, the land of the dead, ruled by Hades and Persephone
barriers.note: not explained; 'house' could be taken literally; 'dread' = terrible, awe-inspiring

paragraphs.paraphrase: Dismayed, Odysseus weeps in bed and wishes he were dead; eventually he asks who will guide him there, since no ship can reach the land of the dead.

Circe says he needs no guide: the North Wind will carry his ship across the waters of Oceanus to Persephone's shore, with its groves of poplars and willows. He should land there and walk to the dark house of Hades, near a rock where the rivers Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus (a branch of the Styx) flow into the Acheron.

barriers.quote: When your ship has crossed the waters of Oceanus
barriers.my_reading: Oceanus here seems to be a vast river or sea at the edge of the world, although in ¶11 it was a person
barriers.note: the double use as a person and as a body of water is confusing

barriers.quote: willows that shed their fruit before its time
barriers.my_reading: trees that drop their fruit unripe, an image of barrenness and death
barriers.note: willows do not obviously bear fruit

barriers.quote: Beach your ship here on the shore of Oceanus
barriers.my_reading: beach your ship there
barriers.note: 'here' where 'there' is meant

barriers.quote: the rivers Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus (which is a branch of the river Styx) flow into the river Acheron
barriers.my_reading: rivers of the underworld that meet at the landmark rock
barriers.note: a cluster of unexplained names; hard to follow, especially aloud

paragraphs.paraphrase: At that spot he must dig a pit about eighteen inches each way and pour into it, for all the dead, honey mixed with milk, then wine, then water, sprinkled with white barley flour. He must pray to the ghosts and promise that, once home in Ithaca, he will sacrifice his best barren heifer and heap the fire with rich offerings, and give Tiresias alone his finest black sheep.

barriers.quote: a barren heifer
barriers.my_reading: a young cow that has not had a calf
barriers.note: 'heifer' is a farming word

barriers.quote: will load the pyre with good things
barriers.my_reading: will pile valuable offerings on a sacrificial fire
barriers.note: 'pyre' = a pile of wood for burning

paragraphs.paraphrase: After praying, he must sacrifice a ram and a black ewe, turning their heads toward Erebus while he himself turns away toward the river. Ghosts will then come; his men must skin the two sheep and burn them as offerings to Hades and Persephone, while he sits with drawn sword keeping the other ghosts away from the blood until Tiresias has come and told him how to sail home.

barriers.quote: bending their heads toward Erebus
barriers.my_reading: turning the animals' heads toward the dark underworld as they are killed
barriers.note: 'Erebus' is never explained; outside knowledge only

barriers.quote: turn away from them yourself as though you were making for the river
barriers.my_reading: as part of the ritual he must face away from the sacrifice, toward the river
barriers.note: unclear which river is meant and why

barriers.quote: keep any other poor ghost from coming near the spilt blood
barriers.my_reading: ghosts are drawn to the sacrificial blood, and Tiresias must reach it first
barriers.note: why the ghosts want the blood is not explained; that they drink it is outside knowledge only

paragraphs.paraphrase: It was dawn when she finished; she dressed him, and put on a fine light robe, a golden belt and a head covering herself. Odysseus went round the house waking the men kindly and telling them they must leave, since Circe had explained everything, and they obeyed.

They did not leave without loss: Elpenor, a young man of little sense or courage, had gone up on the roof to sleep off his drinking; woken by the bustle, he forgot to use the stairs, fell off the roof, broke his neck and died.
Odysseus tells the gathered men that instead of going home they must first go to the land of the dead to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Tiresias.

The men threw themselves down, groaning and tearing their hair, to no avail. When they reached the shore, Circe had brought the ram and the ewe, which they tethered by the ship; she had passed among them unseen, since no one can see a god who does not wish to be seen.

barriers.quote: Circe brought the ram and the ewe, and we made them fast close by the ship
barriers.my_reading: Circe, unseen, brought the two sheep for the sacrifice, and the men tied them up by the ship
barriers.note: 'we made them fast' seems to conflict with 'without our knowing it' in the next sentence

book_level: Formula lines repeat word for word ('When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared', 'to the going down of the sun ... it came on dark', 'glad to have escaped death though we had lost our comrades', 'Odysseus, noble son of Laertes'); readable, but old-fashioned and repetitive aloud.

Many words carry older meanings that mislead a modern reader: 'mess' (a dish), 'meal' (ground grain), 'virtue' (power), 'bound' (obliged), 'fountain' (spring), 'web' (woven cloth), 'mischief' (harm), 'gallery' (covered walkway).
Archaic or specialist vocabulary makes it read more like Victorian than modern English: made fast, laid out, hue and cry, hallooing, beech mast, gambol, lowing, heifer, pyre, herald, flayed.
Gestures of supplication and grief are never explained: sitting on the threshold as suppliants, clasping knees, 'entreated her by her knees', covering and uncovering heads.

The underworld instructions (¶40-44) pile up unexplained names (Hades, Persephone, Tiresias, Oceanus, Styx, Acheron, Cocytus, Pyriphlegethon, Erebus) and ritual steps whose purpose is unclear (the pit, turning away, guarding the blood); Oceanus is a person in ¶11 and a body of water in ¶42.
Circe's threat, 'strip you of your manhood' / 'unman me', is ambiguous: castration, impotence or general weakness?

Small continuity gaps make the reader stop: 'this morning' in ¶13, 'the men who had been left behind' in ¶37, a 'severe reprimand' never shown (¶36), a 'promise' never made on the page (¶39), 'we made them fast' while Circe is unseen (¶48).

The Laestrygonian short-nights detail (¶7) and Aeolus's floating '(as it were)' island are hard to interpret, and the loss of the whole rest of the fleet in ¶10 is stated in one short sentence that is easy to miss.
